business_summary: NVIDIA Corporation is a semiconductor company. The evidence supplied is financial metrics only, with no documents describing products or customers. Revenue grew at a 100% 3-year CAGR to FY26, operating margin was 61.7%, and borrowings are minimal at 0.05x equity.
why_own: The numbers show very fast growth (revenue 3-year CAGR of 100%, net profit 3-year CAGR of 202%) with a 61.7% operating margin, ROCE of 85.5% and almost no debt. No investor documents were supplied, so there are no qualitative drivers, and the thesis rests on reported financials alone; the P/E of 27x has no comparison to its own history.

drivers.statement: Revenue keeps compounding at a high rate: the 3-year revenue CAGR stays well above 40%, against 100% now. (warn line tightened by code from 40 to 70.03.)
Operating margin holds at a high level, above 50%, against 61.7% now. It is up 40.3 points over three years, and whether that level lasts is untested.
Profit converts into cash: cash from operations stays at 0.7x net profit or better, against 0.86x now.
Returns on capital stay very high: ROCE above 50%, against 85.5% now. (warn line tightened by code from 50 to 59.84.)

kill_criteria.description: Operating margin falls below 35%, well under the current 61.7%.
3-year revenue CAGR falls below 15%, which would end the high-growth case.

risks.statement: Valuation is high on book value (price/book 33x) and the P/E of 27x on trailing profit has no comparison to the company's own history, so there is little cushion if growth slows.

Margins rose 40 points in three years and growth rates are extreme (100% revenue CAGR, 202% profit CAGR). Whether these can be sustained is untested in the evidence, and the growth rates will be hard to repeat.
Cash from operations was 0.86x net profit in FY26, below 1x, so reported profit is not fully matched by cash.

skeptic_counter_case: The thesis rests on financials alone: no document describes products, customers or demand, so nothing explains why 100% growth persists. The thesis would be wrong if FY23 was a trough base and margins mean-revert. Margin three years ago was about 21% (61.7 minus 40.3), so both the CAGR and the margin gain are measured from a low start. The kill lines look lenient: margin must fall to 35% (27 points) and the 3-year CAGR to 15% before anything trips. Cash conversion of 0.86x is already below 1x. The P/E of 27x has no history to compare against, and P/B is 33x, so there is little cushion if growth slows. What would change this view: Evidence that the margin and growth are structural, such as documents showing diversified, contracted demand, or several more quarters with operating margin above 50% and cash conversion at or above 1x.
